Twenty allocated identities: planned15 including Friday promotion plus five slots: dormire, camicia, reflexive-pronoun family, a chiave, receptive custode. Preserve custode productive16; no card or typed answer requires it. Missing cardinal bases begin16 under the revised plan; none is used here.

An explicit Thursday-evening bridge opens boxes2–5, selects1–5 by their small/easy books, and hands those exact five numbers to the transport worker before Friday. He copies them onto his own sheet, keeps his pen and gives Paolo his appointment sheet with Friday10. No payment/loading occurs. Friday’s public reading meeting remains at3.

Friday arrivals at current library are7/8/9, following wakes6/7/8. The volunteers coordinate their routines and make a shared appointment10 at the old green door; actual meeting enacts the consequence. Yellow upstairs door stays shut and its room uninspected. Custodian remains late.

Envelope remains addressed to Ada, sealed and contents unknown. Both photos stay with Elena between two sheets. The two unknown photo identities are not disclosed. Marco/chair/clamp/hammer stay at workshop; existing safe library chairs are used, including the chair Paolo offers Ada.

Paolo’s own phone and repair100 euros travel with him; Elena uses a separate ordinary bedside alarm clock and leaves it at home. The transport worker’s own phone is introduced as his at the end and shows the custodian’s message. Library pen is borrowed from its established location under the small sheet and returned beside the other pen.

Five original native SVGs delivered: Thursday-evening cover, night-to-morning/rising/dressing sequence, outside the locked yellow door, seven-cycle week planner, hour/minute grid. Figures remain clothed/covered; Friday Elena wears a white shirt. The minute grid uses the Arabic figure60, not the future Italian cardinal word sessanta, and no unshown Italian number word is required. All media were Cairo-rendered and inspected. Prose and contextual/known-word aids remain readable without pictures. Zero image-generation spend; no audio.

segments.text: Il signore apre le scatole due, tre, quattro e cinque. Ada guarda i libri nelle scatole uno, due, tre, quattro e cinque: sono piccoli e facili. Vuole quei libri per la riunione. Paolo prende la penna del signore e scrive i cinque numeri sul suo foglio. Il signore prende la penna e li scrive sul suo foglio; sul foglio di Paolo scrive: «Domani, alle dieci». Restituisce il foglio a Paolo. È sera; i cinque numeri sono con il signore prima di venerdì. Le nove scatole sono ancora qui; Paolo tiene tutti i cento euro.

segments.text: La mattina Elena si sveglia alle sei. Non dorme: guarda la sveglia e la finestra. Oggi è venerdì. Elena ha bisogno dei libri per la riunione alle tre, ma prima vuole cercare la stanza di sopra. La sveglia non è il telefono di Paolo: è sopra il tavolo della sua camera. Paolo ha il suo telefono a casa sua.

Il signore prende il suo telefono e mostra un messaggio del custode: «Alle dieci». Ma il custode non è qui; è tardi. Paolo aspetta cinque minuti, dopo aspetta altri cinque minuti. «Ci incontriamo tutti alla stessa ora, ma manca ancora una persona», risponde Elena. Ada non apre la sua busta. La porta gialla è chiusa a chiave; il custode ha la chiave e non arriva. La porta gialla è ancora chiusa.

grammar.title: Grammatica
grammar.rule: io mi sveglio; tu ti svegli; Elena si sveglia; noi ci svegliamo; voi vi svegliate; Elena e Paolo si svegliano
grammar.note_en:
The short pronouns in this chapter belong to the verb’s subject, the person or people whose action or change is being described. With a reflexive meaning, the action concerns that same person rather than a separate recipient. Some Italian verbs use this pronoun as part of their ordinary meaning: waking up and getting up describe a change of state, not a deliberate action performed on a separate person. Their dictionary forms end in -si; the tables give only the forms actually read in this story.

The rule and first table show all six present-tense person patterns. Io mi sveglio means “I wake up”; tu ti svegli means “you wake up”, for one familiar person; Elena si sveglia means “Elena wakes up”; noi ci svegliamo means “we wake up”; voi vi svegliate means “you wake up”, for more than one person; Elena e Paolo si svegliano means “Elena and Paolo wake up”. The table caption Persona / Forma means “person / form”. The subject, pronoun and verb ending work together. Mi, ti, ci and vi are linked to the first and second persons. Si occurs with both a singular third-person subject and a plural third-person subject; the verb distinguishes sveglia, “wakes up”, from svegliano, “wake up”. The pronoun does not change with the subject’s gender.

The second table gives other attested combinations. Elena si alza means “Elena gets up”; Elena si veste means “Elena gets dressed”; Paolo si siede means “Paolo sits down”. These are actions or changes, rather than simply the resulting position. The familiar adjective for being seated describes a position; the new verb describes the act of sitting down. Earlier chapters taught that adjective; this chapter develops the verb. Noi ci sediamo means “we sit down”; noi ci incontriamo means “we meet”; voi vi incontrate means “you meet”, addressed to more than one person; le tre persone si incontrano means “the three people meet”. Forma, the second caption, means “form”. The irregular change siede / sediamo is shown because both forms occur in the story; no unseen forms of this verb are required in the exercises.

Meeting has a reciprocal meaning: the people meet one another. In ci incontriamo, “we meet”, ci refers to the people included in we. It does not mean that each person meets themself. The group can wake up at different times and still arrange to meet at the same place and time. The present tense can describe a regular routine as well as a present event or an arrangement: the dialogue compares usual wake-up times, and the final scene enacts the shared appointment.

These uses differ from the indirect recipients in chapter14. Il signore gli telefona means “the man phones him”: gli points to the custodian, someone other than the caller. In mi sveglio, “I wake up”, mi belongs with the speaker’s own change of state. The verb and its meaning determine the pronoun’s job; the same spelling does not by itself identify a reflexive, reciprocal or indirect-object use. This chapter keeps ordinary pronouns before finite present-tense verbs and does not introduce combined object pronouns or commands.
